cards.front: What do right-of-way rules decide and does anyone own the right of way
cards.back: Right-of-way rules set who yields first and the order for entering and crossing intersections, yet nobody ever owns the right of way automatically, so every approach demands a fresh read of the scene.

cards.front: Who do you yield to at an intersection, on a left turn, and at a simultaneous four-way stop
cards.back: Yield to the driver who arrived first, to opposing traffic including right-turning vehicles when you turn left, and to the driver on your right when both of you reach a four-way stop at once.

cards.front: Who do you yield to when entering from a driveway, minor road, or ramp
cards.back: Yield to highway traffic when pulling out of a driveway or private road, to main-road drivers when joining from a minor road, to freeway traffic already rolling when you enter from a ramp, and to any pedestrian, cyclist, or driver still inside the intersection.

cards.front: What devices control traffic and whose orders overrule signs and signals
cards.back: Control devices span signals, signs, pavement markings, and live direction from officers, highway crews, and school guards, and an officer's orders overrule every sign and signal where two roads meet.

cards.front: Who wins at an intersection by arrival and at a simultaneous four-way stop
cards.back: First arrival wins the intersection, while a simultaneous four-way stop gives the nod to the driver on your right.

cards.front: How are stacked and horizontal signals ordered
cards.back: Stacked signals read red over yellow over green from the top, while horizontal city signals read red left, yellow center, and green right, with lone single-color lights posted at some spots.
cards.memory_hook: Red top or left, green bottom

cards.front: What does a green light allow and what does a left on green still wait for
cards.back: A green light lets you go straight or turn after yielding to everyone lawfully in the intersection, and a left on green still waits for opposing through traffic.

cards.front: What does a steady yellow mean and when is entering on red illegal
cards.back: Yellow warns the signal is turning red, so stop when you safely can; clearing the box on red after a yellow entry is lawful, but entering after red is against the law.
cards.memory_hook: Yellow warns, enter after red illegal

cards.front: Where do you stop on red and when may you turn right
cards.back: On red, stop behind the crosswalk or stop line until green, then turn right when the way is clear of cars and pedestrians unless a sign bans it.
cards.memory_hook: Stop behind line, right when clear

cards.front: When is a left on red legal and which lane does a one-way turn use
cards.back: Left on red is legal only from a one-way street onto another one-way street after a full stop and a clear road, and any one-way turn lands in the nearest lane running your direction.

cards.front: What do a flashing yellow and a flashing red each order
cards.back: A flashing yellow orders slower speed and a sharp watch at crossings, work areas, and service trucks, while a flashing red demands a full stop before moving through clear space.
cards.memory_hook: Flash yellow slow, flash red stop

cards.front: What do twin flashing reds at a railroad crossing order and how is the crossbuck treated
cards.back: Twin flashing reds guard a railroad crossing, so stop until the flashing ends and no train nears, and treat the nearby crossbuck exactly like a yield sign.

cards.front: What do steady green, flashing yellow, upward green, and red arrows each mean
cards.back: A steady green arrow sends you that way from the proper lane, a flashing yellow arrow urges a careful proceed, an upward green arrow means straight ahead, and a red arrow bans that turn until green, always obeying the head above your lane.
cards.memory_hook: Green go, flashing careful, red banned

cards.front: How does a steady yellow differ from a flashing yellow
cards.back: A steady yellow means the light is turning red, while a flashing yellow only orders slower speed and a sharper watch.

cards.front: How does a flashing yellow differ from a flashing red
cards.back: Flashing yellow asks for caution, while flashing red demands a full stop before proceeding through clear space.

cards.front: How does right on red differ from left on red
cards.back: Right on red follows any legal stop, while left on red works only from a one-way street onto another one-way street.

cards.front: How does a steady green arrow differ from a flashing yellow arrow
cards.back: A steady green arrow grants the turn from the proper lane, while a flashing yellow arrow only permits a careful proceed.

cards.front: What does the round yellow railroad board warn and what does the white crossbuck order
cards.back: A round yellow board with an X and black railroad letters warns of tracks ahead, so slow down, look, listen, and ready a stop, while the white X that reads Railroad Crossing at the tracks orders a stop behind the line until the way clears.

cards.front: What does a posted track count warn and why check every track yourself
cards.back: A posted track count warns that several trains may cross, yet many multi-track crossings carry no such sign and some crossings lack lights entirely, so check every track in both directions yourself.
cards.memory_hook: Count may be missing, check all

cards.front: How do you cross rails, when do you wait, and where do you stop if traffic forces it
cards.back: Cross rails briskly without stopping after looking both ways, wait while a train passes or until gates and lights release you, and when traffic forces a stop, halt at the line ahead of the rails.
cards.memory_hook: Cross briskly, wait gates, stop line

cards.front: What do you do if your car stalls on the tracks
cards.back: Stalled or boxed on the tracks, leave the car at once and run toward the oncoming train and away from the rails to dodge flying debris, then from a safe distance call the eight hundred number by the crossbuck or call nine one one, and never restart until a dispatcher says it is safe.
cards.memory_hook: Leave car, run toward train, call

cards.front: How far may a freight train need to stop and how do you cross multi-track rails
cards.back: A freight train at fifty-five miles per hour may need a mile or more to stop, so after one train passes on multi-track rails, wait for a clear view both ways, cross only with room to clear fully, and never stop on the crossing.
cards.memory_hook: Mile to stop, wait clear view

cards.front: What should you expect at every crossing and what does passing lowered gates cost
cards.back: Expect a train at every crossing, because rolling past flashing warnings or lowered gates breaks the law and earns a citation.
cards.memory_hook: Expect a train, gates mean citation

cards.front: Which railroad sign warns and which orders the stop
cards.back: The round yellow advance board warns of tracks ahead, while the white X crossbuck at the rails orders the stop itself.

cards.front: What color and shape are warning signs and when is fluorescent yellow used
cards.back: Warning signs flag possible danger ahead in black on yellow diamonds, urging slower speed and stop readiness, with fluorescent yellow reserved for school zones, school crossings, and pedestrian crossings.

cards.front: What do orange work-zone signs mark and what must you obey there
cards.back: Orange diamond or rectangular work-zone boards mark construction, maintenance, and emergency work with warnings of crews, slower speeds, detours, slow equipment, and shifting surfaces, so obey flaggers and signs, follow drums, cones, tubes, and temporary signals, and stop at any white line.

cards.front: How do you give road workers a brake and what happens to work-zone speeding fines
cards.back: Give road workers a brake by slowing down, staying ready for sudden stops, refusing to tailgate, and remembering that work-zone speeding fines double.

cards.front: What do regulatory signs look like and what does a red ring and slash mean
cards.back: Regulatory signs speak the law in white squares, rectangles, or special shapes with black, red, or green markings, covering direction, lanes, turns, speed, and parking, with a red ring and slash banning the pictured act, while black-and-white speed boards cap legal speed for ideal conditions.

cards.front: What do the stop sign and the yield sign each look like and order
cards.back: An eight-sided red stop sign with white letters orders a stop behind the line or crosswalk plus a yield to crossing traffic and walkers in every direction, and a red-and-white downward triangle yield sign orders slowing until right-of-way traffic passes.

cards.front: What do shared center lane, one-way, wrong-way, and do-not-enter signs each mean
cards.back: A shared center lane serves left turns from either side only and never through traffic or passing, one-way signs permit travel in the arrow's direction alone, wrong-way signs warn you are headed against traffic at ramps and one-way starts, and do-not-enter signs bar entry at those same spots.

cards.front: How does a stop sign differ from a yield sign
cards.back: The eight-sided red stop sign orders a complete halt, while the downward red-and-white triangle only orders slowing for right-of-way traffic.

cards.front: How do white, yellow, and green, brown, or blue signs differ in purpose
cards.back: White regulatory boards state laws you must obey, while yellow diamonds warn of danger and green, brown, or blue guides inform and direct.
cards.memory_hook: White law, yellow warn, guides inform

decks.module: Guide signs, markings, colors and shapes

cards.front: What colors are guide signs and where do they point
cards.back: Guide signs in green, brown, or blue squares and rectangles point to crossing roads, towns, sights, hospitals, fuel, food, and lodging.

cards.front: What do route shields show and how should you use them
cards.back: Route shields use shape and color to name interstate, federal, state, city, county, and local roads, so map your route first and then trail the shields through strange country.

cards.front: What do painted lines, arrows, words, and symbols on the pavement do
cards.back: Painted lines, arrows, words, and symbols split lanes, govern passing and lane changes, assign turn lanes, outline walkways, and mark stop points for signs and signals.

cards.front: Where do you halt at a crosswalk, whom do you yield to, and what if no crossing shows
cards.back: Crosswalks frame legal pedestrian crossings, so halt behind the stop line, crosswalk, or sign and yield to anyone entering or inside, stay wary since many crossings lack paint, stop ahead of the intersection when no crossing shows, and honor a stop line before the crosswalk first.

cards.front: What do the standard sign colors red, green, and yellow mean
cards.back: Standard sign colors read red for stop or forbidden, green for permitted movement and guidance, and yellow for general warning.
cards.memory_hook: Red stop, green go, yellow warn

cards.front: What do the standard sign shapes each signal
cards.back: Standard shapes read horizontal rectangle for guides, lone triangle for yield, vertical rectangle for regulation, diamond for present or possible hazards, pentagon for schools, and round for railroad and advance warning.
cards.memory_hook: Diamond hazard, pentagon school, round rail

cards.front: Which shapes serve yield, hazards, schools, and railroads
cards.back: Triangles serve yield alone, diamonds mark present or possible hazards, pentagons mark schools, and round boards warn of railroads.

cards.front: What does each of red, green, and yellow signal on a sign
cards.back: Red stops or forbids, green permits movement and guides, and yellow warns in general.
cards.memory_hook: Red forbids, green permits, yellow warns

recap_hooks.text: Nobody owns right of way, first arrival wins, officers overrule
Green goes, yellow warns, red stops, right on red when clear
Round warns, crossbuck stops, stalled means run toward train
Yellow warns, orange works, white regulates, eight sides stop

recap_hooks.text: Guides inform, paint governs, colors and shapes tell purpose
